opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the "Squid Game" framing captures how a lot of people see the AI race right now: everyone is competing in one arena, there's a single leaderboard, and only one player walks out alive. If you lose on one benchmark, you're eliminated. I don't think that's a healthy way to think about it, and I don't think it's how progress actually happens.

First, AI is not a zero-sum game. The space of problems is enormous. Language models are one direction, but physical AI, robotics, autonomous driving, world models, and scientific discovery are wide open. Most of the value AI will create hasn't been unlocked yet. When the pie is growing that fast, it doesn't make sense to act as if there's only one slice and everybody has to fight to the death for it.

Second, progress in this field has always been cumulative. Think about the ingredients we rely on today: convolutional networks, transformers, diffusion models, GANs, large-scale pretraining. They came from many different groups, academia and industry, across many countries, building on each other's papers and open-source code. If everybody had treated research like a deadly game where you hide everything and try to eliminate rivals, we'd be much further behind. Openness, sharing models, sharing data recipes: that's what accelerates everyone, including yourself.

Third, the Squid Game mindset pushes people to optimize for the wrong things. If survival depends on topping one leaderboard this month, you chase short-term benchmark numbers instead of tackling hard, long-horizon problems. For something like physical AI, you need patience. You need to build the data pipelines, the simulation infrastructure, the evaluation methods, before a breakthrough is even possible. That's very hard to do if you feel you'll be eliminated in the next round.

And finally, I think of the ecosystem more like a platform than a battlefield. Part of why we release models openly is that we want developers, startups, and researchers to build on them. Their success is our success. A robotics startup that fine-tunes a world model for its own warehouse isn't a competitor to eliminate; it's someone who expands what the technology can do.

So competition is good. It drives everyone to be better. But it should be more like a sports league, or even a scientific community, where you push hard, you learn from your rivals, and the whole field keeps getting stronger. Not a game where only one person survives and everyone else disappears.

r001.rationale: The response describes one arena and a single leaderboard, but does not clearly say that everyone is trying to solve exactly the same problem.

r002.rationale: It says the space of problems is enormous, names several open areas, and argues that growing value gives competitors more than one slice to pursue.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the Squid Game framing assumes a zero-sum world: a fixed pot of prize money, and every player eliminated makes the remaining players richer. That's just not how I see AI. The pie is not fixed. We're still at the very beginning, and the total value that models can create, in robotics, in simulation, in healthcare, in content, is so much larger than what any single lab can capture that the "last one standing" mindset actually makes everyone poorer.

At NVIDIA, where I've worked on generative models and now on world models with Cosmos, I see this very concretely. When another lab releases a strong open model or a new technique, our work doesn't get worse. We learn from it, we build on it, and the whole field moves. A lot of what I've done in my career, from GANs to image synthesis to the simulation work, exists because other people published and shared. If everyone treated every result like a secret weapon in an elimination game, progress would slow dramatically.

The second thing is that Squid Game is about survival of individuals, and AI is really about ecosystems. You need the chip makers, the model builders, the application developers, the researchers in universities, the open-source community. These are not competitors in one arena; they're layers that depend on each other. If one layer "wins" by killing the others, it loses, because it has nothing to stand on.

And finally, there's a human cost to that framing. When you make it a death match, people start optimizing for not losing instead of for doing good science. They stop publishing, stop sharing data, stop collaborating across companies and countries. I think the best years of this field came from openness, and I'd rather see competition that pushes everyone to be better, more like a very intense marathon, than a game where the goal is to make the other person disappear.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI competition as non-zero-sum and rejects an elimination mindset, but it does not say competitors are all trying to solve exactly the same problem.

r002.rationale: It says the pie is not fixed and that models can create value across robotics, simulation, healthcare, and content—far more than any single lab can capture—making expansive opportunities a reason to reject the Squid Game framing.

astra-6.text:
I think the problem with that analogy is that it assumes there can only be one winner, and everyone else has to lose. I don’t think AI works that way. Different models can serve different needs, and there’s room for many teams to create something valuable.

Competition is good—it pushes us to make models better and more useful. But we also benefit from shared progress: researchers publishing ideas, people building on each other’s work, and developers finding applications we didn’t anticipate. You can compete and still contribute to that ecosystem.

Ultimately, the question shouldn’t just be, “Did my model beat your model?” It should be, “Are we building something that helps people?” That’s a much bigger opportunity than a game with one survivor.

r001.rationale: The response says models can serve different needs; it does not characterize Squid Game-like competition as everyone trying to solve the same problem.

r002.rationale: It mentions different needs and room for many teams to create value, but does not clearly identify an abundance of valuable problems to solve as the reason.

sol-6.1.text:
I think competition is healthy, but it shouldn’t mean that everyone else has to disappear for you to succeed. AI is a very broad field. Different models can serve different needs, and there’s room for many teams to create value.

If we treat it like Squid Game, where there can be only one survivor, we put too much emphasis on beating each other and too little on what we’re actually building for people. I’d rather see competition that pushes us to make models more useful, more accessible, and more reliable, while still allowing researchers to share ideas. You can compete and contribute to a shared foundation at the same time.

r001.rationale: The response says there is room for different models and teams, but does not characterize Squid Game–like competition as everyone trying to solve exactly the same problem.

r002.rationale: It describes AI as a broad field with different needs and says many teams can create value, expressing that there are multiple valuable areas for competition.
